title: Data structures library with tests and benchmarks
summary: Core data structures implemented from scratch with a clean API, thorough tests and benchmarks that check your Big-O claims against real timings.
why: It shows you understand what happens inside the structures that coding interviews are built on, and that you back claims with evidence. Benchmarks plus tests read as engineering maturity, not homework.
brief:
Write a small library (call it something like `pyds`) with a dynamic array, a singly linked list, a stack, a queue, a hash map with separate chaining and resizing, a binary min-heap and a binary search tree. Each structure gets a documented interface, type hints and a docstring that states the time complexity of every operation.

Constraints: don't wrap Python's built-in list or dict as the core storage of the structure you are implementing (a fixed-size Python list may stand in for a raw array). Make the structures feel like Python containers where it makes sense (`len`, `in`, iteration). Raise clear exceptions for invalid operations, such as popping from an empty heap.

The twist that makes this a portfolio piece is evidence. Write tests, including property-based tests (for example with Hypothesis) that run thousands of random operations against your structure and a built-in and check they always agree. Then write benchmarks that time operations at growing sizes and plot the results, so you can show your hash map lookups staying flat while a list scan grows linearly.

milestones.title: Linear structures
tasks: Dynamic array with amortized O(1) append and capacity doubling
Singly linked list with push_front, append, remove and reverse
Stack and queue, with O(1) enqueue and dequeue
milestones.doneWhen: Each structure passes unit tests for empty, single-element and many-element cases.

milestones.title: Hash map
tasks: Separate chaining with a load factor threshold that triggers a resize
get, put, delete, contains and iteration over keys
Updating an existing key and deleting a missing key behave like dict
milestones.doneWhen: A property-based test runs 10,000 random operations against your map and a dict, and they always agree.

milestones.title: Heap and binary search tree
tasks: Binary min-heap with push, pop and heapify from a list
Binary search tree with insert, search, delete (all three cases) and in-order traversal
Heapsort built on your heap, checked against sorted()
milestones.doneWhen: Tests cover deleting a node with zero, one and two children, and heapsort matches sorted() on random inputs.

milestones.title: Benchmarks
tasks: Time key operations at sizes from 1,000 to 1,000,000 with timeit
Plot time against n with matplotlib and save the charts
Compare against the built-ins and explain the gap
milestones.doneWhen: The repository contains charts for each structure, and the README says whether each operation matched its predicted Big-O.

milestones.title: Documentation and CI
tasks: Write a README with the API, a complexity table and the charts
Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the tests on every push
Run a type checker such as mypy in CI
milestones.doneWhen: CI is green on the main branch, and the README's complexity table matches the docstrings.

stretch: A self-balancing tree (AVL or red-black) and a benchmark that shows why it matters on sorted input
An open-addressing hash map compared with your chaining version
An LRU cache built from your hash map and a doubly linked list
Port two structures to TypeScript with the same tests
rubric: A reviewer should see each operation's time complexity documented and matching the implementation
A reviewer should see randomized or property-based tests comparing each structure with a built-in
A reviewer should see edge cases tested: empty structures, single elements, duplicates and resize boundaries
A reviewer should see benchmark charts and an honest explanation of any result that did not match theory
A reviewer should see no built-in list or dict used as the core storage of the structure being implemented
A reviewer should see green CI and type hints throughout
showcase: README: a table of structures and operation complexities, the benchmark charts, how to run tests and benchmarks, and a 'Surprises' section about results that differed from theory
Put the clearest chart (for example hash map lookup versus list scan) at the top of the README
Pin the repository and mention the property-based testing in its description
resumeBullet: Implemented 7 core data structures in Python from scratch with 150+ unit and property-based tests, and benchmarked them up to 1M elements to confirm their Big-O behavior, with charts in the README.
interviewTalkingPoints: Why dynamic array append is amortized O(1) even though some appends copy every element
How you chose a load factor and what happens to performance during a resize
A bug that property-based testing caught and example-based tests missed
A benchmark that surprised you, and why (constant factors, memory effects, interpreter overhead)
